Learn the method • Practise small skills • Plan ideas • Write complete essays

This guide takes you from understanding a question to writing and revising a complete essay. Work through the four parts in order the first time. Afterwards, use the topic plans and models to practise the skills you find most difficult.

Use a notebook or a separate Word page for longer answers. The short response lines in this guide are for planning and brief exercises. Vietnamese notes explain selected terms; write your final essays in English.
Your learning route

rows: Learn question types, paragraph development and useful language.
Practise sentences, paragraphs, introductions and vocabulary.
Use a planning worksheet and 25 topic practice prompts.
Draft essays, study 14 worked models and revise your work.
Review key terms and official test guidance.
Check every exercise and all 25 practice essays.

theory.text: A manageable study routine

Session 1: Read one theory page and explain the method in your own words. Session 2: Complete the related short exercises and check the answers. Session 3: Plan two essays without writing them. Session 4: Write one essay, review it and rewrite the weakest paragraph.

Repeat this cycle with new topics. Start untimed, then reduce your writing time gradually. Progress when you can complete each stage independently; reading a model is not the same as being able to write one.
How to use the examples

Attempt each task before reading its suggested answer. The plans and essays show possible approaches, not compulsory opinions or scripts to memorise. The model essays are learning examples, not examiner awarded band scores.
Part 1 Theory
Understand what the question asks
Task 2 requires at least 250 words. Allow about 40 minutes and write connected paragraphs in an academic or neutral style. Relevant examples can come from your knowledge or experience. [1]

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “Some people think cities should spend more on public transport than roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?” A relevant thesis is: “I largely agree because better transit can serve more commuters, although road maintenance remains necessary.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The question requests a JUDGEMENT, not a list of the causes of traffic jams. Underline “spend more”, “public transport than roads” and “extent”. Those words determine both the comparison you must make and the position you should maintain.
Read the instruction before choosing a structure

rows: To what extent do you agree or disagree?
State how far you agree and support that position.
Two reasons, or a concession followed by your main argument.
Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Explain both positions fairly and make your own view clear.
View A; view B, with your judgement integrated.
Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
Discuss benefits and drawbacks, then compare their importance.
Benefits; drawbacks; explain which matters more.
What are the causes and solutions?
Explain why the issue occurs and how it could be addressed.
Causes; solutions matched to those causes.
What problems arise and what solutions are possible?
Explain consequences and propose relevant responses.
Problems; solutions matched to those problems.
What are the reasons and effects?
Answer both questions, including an opinion if requested.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Compare these tasks: A) “Discuss both views and give your opinion.” B) “What problems does this cause, and how can they be solved?” The topic in both might be urban traffic, but the required answers are different.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  For A, give a fair explanation of each view plus your position. For B, name specific problems and match each with a mechanism-based solution. Copying an “advantages/disadvantages” outline into either task would omit an explicit instruction and weaken Task Response.
Avoid answering a nearby question

Cause = why something happens. Problem or effect = what happens because of it. Solution = what someone can do. For example, long working hours can be a cause of poor work life balance; weaker family relationships can be an effect; protected time off can be a solution.

These are study categories, not fixed official templates. Follow the exact wording if a question combines categories. “Discuss the advantages and disadvantages” does not ask the same thing as “Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?”
Before writing, identify the topic, the limits of the question, every instruction and any strong word such as all, only or best.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Task: “Why do employees struggle to balance work and family life, and what measures could help?” Off-target point: “Office jobs are becoming popular.” On-target point: “Unpredictable shifts can disrupt childcare arrangements; employers could publish rotas earlier.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The on-target point identifies a CAUSE and then a plausible SOLUTION. Popularity of office work may be true but does not answer either demand. Before drafting, write two tiny labels beside your plan: “Why?” and “What helps?”
Build an essay and a clear paragraph

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “Should schools teach financial skills?” Plan: Introduction—agree; Body 1—budgeting prevents avoidable mistakes; Body 2—schools offer equal access; Conclusion—restate the case.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The structure makes the argument traceable. Each body paragraph has a distinct job, rather than mixing five benefits into two undeveloped lists. A different organisation is acceptable if each part still contributes to the answer.
Give each paragraph a job
Introduction: paraphrase the issue accurately and give your position or direct answer. Avoid a long general opening.
Body paragraph 1: develop one main point relevant to the task.
Body paragraph 2: develop the next main point. Add a third body paragraph only if it has a clear purpose.
Conclusion: bring your answer together and restate your position. Do not introduce an undeveloped new argument.
A four paragraph essay is a useful starting point. There is no requirement to use exactly four paragraphs or exactly two ideas in each body paragraph.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Essay question: “Should public libraries remain free?” Introduction: clear agreement. Body 1: free access supports lower-income learners. Body 2: libraries offer public benefits such as information access. Conclusion: summarise why free provision is justified.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Label the role of every paragraph before writing. If a sentence about library architecture appears in Body 1 and does not explain access for learners, remove or relocate it. This is a practical test of paragraph unity and coherence.
Develop rather than list
Use this flexible sequence: main point → explanation → example or detail → result or link to the question. Vietnamese reminder: nêu ý → giải thích → ví dụ → kết quả hoặc liên hệ đề bài.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Weak: “Online learning is flexible, cheap, modern and effective.” Developed: “Online lessons allow employees to study after work, so they can gain qualifications without giving up paid hours. For example, a nurse may watch recorded lectures around rotating shifts.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The revised point chooses ONE benefit (flexibility), explains the mechanism (scheduling) and offers an illustrative scenario. Its quality comes from cause-and-effect detail, not from adding more adjectives or unrelated points.
Annotated example on studying abroad
Main point: Studying abroad can help students become more independent.
Explanation: Living away from their families means they must manage tasks that their parents may previously have handled.
Example: For instance, a student may need to arrange accommodation, manage a monthly budget and resolve problems with a landlord.
Result: Repeatedly making these decisions can build confidence and practical skills that remain useful after graduation.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Paragraph logic: “Living abroad increases independence” → “students handle daily decisions” → “they must find accommodation and budget” → “these decisions develop practical confidence.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Underline the FIRST sentence as the main point. The second answers “why?”, the third answers “what would that look like?”, and the fourth links the scenario back to the claimed benefit. Each sentence earns its place through a distinct function.
Turn the notes into a paragraph

Studying abroad can help students become more independent. Living away from their families means they must manage tasks that their parents may previously have handled. For instance, a student may need to arrange accommodation, manage a monthly budget and resolve problems with a landlord. Repeatedly making these decisions can build confidence and practical skills that remain useful after graduation.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Notes: “bike lanes → safer routes → parents allow cycling → fewer short car trips.” Paragraph: “Protected bike lanes can make commuting safer. When traffic is separated from cyclists, parents may be more willing to let older children cycle to school. This could reduce some short car journeys.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Notes are not an essay until the relations are made explicit in grammatical sentences. Notice how “when” expresses the condition and “this” points to the whole preceding result. Do not force all notes into one overloaded sentence.
When a paragraph contains two related ideas

A broader topic sentence can introduce two benefits, such as career opportunities and independence. Develop each one, rather than giving both a single sentence. If your paragraph becomes crowded, choose one stronger idea and explain it fully.
Check: Can you underline one main point? Does each later sentence explain it? Is the example relevant? A final summary sentence is optional when the result already makes the point clear.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Topic sentence: “Community gardens can improve city life both socially and environmentally.” Detail A: neighbours cooperate to maintain shared plots. Detail B: plants provide limited green space in dense neighbourhoods.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The topic sentence prepares the reader for TWO related strands. Develop each with a mechanism; do not mention friendship, air quality, tourism, exercise and property prices with no explanation. If one strand needs much more room, use a separate paragraph.
Develop and test your supporting ideas
Choose the method that helps your reader understand the point. You do not need all five methods in every paragraph.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “Local buses should be subsidised.” Possible support: show the reason (lower fares), the expected effect (better access to work), and the limitation (funding costs).

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Choose development methods that test the claim instead of stacking generic opinions. In this case, explain why fares matter and acknowledge costs only if it helps your final judgement. A hypothetical but realistic scenario is stronger than fabricated statistics.
1 Give a reason and a result

Point: Technology can improve workplace productivity. Reason: Shared online documents let colleagues update the same project without sending repeated attachments. Result: Teams can spend less time coordinating and more time completing the work.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “Schools should teach basic budgeting.” Reason: many teenagers start managing allowances or part-time earnings before leaving home. Result: they may be less likely to spend essential money impulsively.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The middle step explains WHY the proposal could help; the last step describes WHAT follows. Without the mechanism, “budgeting is useful” merely repeats the thesis. Use cautious verbs such as “may” where the result is plausible rather than guaranteed.
2 Give an example and explain its importance

Example: A factory may use a conveyor belt to move packages between workstations. Explanation: This reduces repetitive carrying and allows workers to focus on quality checks. The example is useful because it shows how the time saving happens.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “Flexible working can improve staff retention.” Illustration: an employee who cares for a parent might work earlier hours and avoid resigning. Follow-up: this arrangement enables the employee to meet care responsibilities while keeping the job.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The example is not self-explanatory. The final sentence explicitly connects the person’s choice to the employment outcome. In Task 2, plausible everyday scenarios work without named companies, research studies or made-up survey figures.
3 Consider what would happen without it

Without shared digital records, staff might have to enter the same information into several files. This could create extra work and inconsistent records. A hypothetical example is acceptable when it is clearly presented as a possibility; do not invent survey results or precise statistics.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “A reliable bus network helps job seekers.” Counterfactual: “Without affordable buses, people who cannot drive may have to reject jobs too far from home.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The phrase “without affordable buses” isolates the missing condition, and “may have to reject jobs” makes the consequence concrete. Counterfactuals strengthen an argument when the imagined alternative is realistic; do not present it as measured evidence.
4 Make a focused comparison

Compared with a paper filing system, a searchable database can make records easier to retrieve. Keep the comparison on the same feature. Comparing manual knitting with a sewing machine, for example, confuses different production processes.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “Electronic health records can improve administrative efficiency.” Comparison: “Unlike paper folders, digital records can be searched from several authorised departments without carrying the same file between offices.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Both sides are compared on THE SAME FUNCTION: accessing a patient record. Do not compare the cost of one system with the speed of the other and treat that as proof. A focused comparison makes the mechanism visible and logically testable.
5 Acknowledge a limitation and respond

Concession: Automated equipment can break down. Response: Maintenance and trained technicians can reduce interruptions, although they cannot eliminate them. Judgement: Productivity gains may still justify the investment where output is high.

Counterargument = an opposing reason. Refutation = your response to that reason. A concession accepts a valid limitation. These techniques can strengthen an argument, but using a counterargument after every idea often makes an essay repetitive.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Concession: “Free university tuition would require substantial public funding.” Response: “Nevertheless, targeted grants for low-income applicants may improve access at a lower overall cost.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The concession accepts an important obstacle; the response adjusts the proposal instead of pretending no cost exists. Such nuance can strengthen a position, but keep the response aligned with the question. Do not add a counterargument solely to sound sophisticated.
Make solutions specific

Weak: The government should raise awareness. Stronger: Local authorities could run food waste campaigns that demonstrate meal planning and storage. If households buy appropriate quantities, less food may be discarded.

Use actor → action → mechanism → expected effect. Then ask whether the solution addresses the cause you identified. “More education” is too vague until you name the audience, content and delivery method.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Vague: “Cities should educate the public about littering.” Specific: “Councils could place illustrated sorting signs next to recycling bins in crowded stations, making it easier for commuters to dispose of packaging correctly.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Identify WHO acts (councils), WHAT they do (install signs), WHERE or TO WHOM (stations/commuters), HOW it works (clear sorting cues), and the intended result (less incorrectly discarded waste). The chain shows how to turn a slogan into a solution.
Use language that makes the logic clear
Learn phrases with their grammar and meaning. Similar expressions are not always interchangeable. Accurate, natural wording is more useful than a long list of impressive synonyms.

rows: lead to + noun; cause + noun; cause someone to + verb
Poor planning can lead to food waste.
contribute to + noun or ing form
Advertising may contribute to unnecessary spending.
Long hours may be associated with work stress.
enable someone to + verb; help someone to + verb
Online courses enable students to study remotely.
benefit + noun; be beneficial to + noun
harm + noun; put something at risk; worsen + problem
Untreated waste can put water quality at risk.
The system saves time, thereby reducing delays.
Although it is convenient, it can be expensive.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Compare “Remote work causes everyone to be healthier” with “Remote work may reduce commuting stress for some employees.” The second claim is narrower and defensible.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Good Task 2 vocabulary conveys the correct strength of an idea. “May”, “some” and “reduce” prevent the absolute claim from exceeding the evidence; do not choose the strongest verb simply because it sounds academic.
Keep the strength of the meaning

“Associated with” describes a relationship; it does not prove that one thing causes another. “Contribute to” usually describes one of several causes. Do not replace these phrases with “the main cause” unless that stronger claim is justified.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Source idea: “Heavy screen use is associated with lower sleep quality in some teenagers.” Appropriate paraphrase: “Frequent screen use may be linked to poorer sleep among certain teenagers.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Linked to” keeps the source’s association and “may” reflects uncertainty. The rewrite “Phones cause insomnia in all children” changes both the causal force and population. Precision is part of Lexical Resource and a prerequisite for valid reasoning.
Control grammar and punctuation

Correct: Many students use online courses; therefore, they can study at flexible times. Also correct: Many students use online courses. Therefore, they can study at flexible times. Avoid joining two complete sentences with only a comma.
“Thereby” introduces a result: Automation reduces repetitive work, thereby freeing staff for other tasks. Check that the result logically follows from the preceding action.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Incorrect: “Public transport is cheaper, it reduces congestion.” Correct: “Public transport can be cheaper, and it may help reduce congestion.” Also correct: “Public transport can be cheaper; it may also help reduce congestion.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The original joins two independent clauses with a comma. The revision either adds a coordinating conjunction or uses a semicolon. “Can” and “may” also avoid guaranteeing effects that depend on local conditions.
Paraphrase accurately

“University places regardless of financial background” concerns fair access. It does not necessarily mean free university for everyone. Likewise, “function” is broader than interior decoration, and “endangered” does not mean already extinct.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “Should employers allow staff to work remotely?” Safe: “Should companies permit employees to carry out their jobs away from the workplace?” Unsafe: “Should all employees permanently abandon offices?”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The original says “allow”, not “require”, and does not specify full-time work or every job. A good paraphrase changes wording while retaining the scope. Keep necessary words if synonyms introduce a new condition.
Handle opinion questions carefully
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: “To what extent should governments restrict car use in city centres?” Position: “I support restrictions in the busiest areas but not a blanket ban.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  This is a qualified but clear position. Body paragraphs must give reasons for targeted restrictions and explain why a total ban could be unfair or impractical. “Some people agree and others disagree” is not your own answer.
A single claim

For “Dangerous sports should be banned”, decide whether you support a ban and how far. You may disagree because safety regulation is preferable, while accepting that the risks are real. Keep that position consistent throughout the essay.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Claim: “Competitive sports should be compulsory at school.” Thesis: “I disagree with compulsory competition because it can exclude less athletic pupils, although optional competitions offer benefits.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The thesis takes a direct position on COMPULSION, not on whether sport itself is good. The concession about voluntary events is relevant because it supports an alternative policy while preserving the disagreement.
Two linked claims

For “It is impossible to help everyone, so governments should focus on their own citizens”, separate the factual claim from the proposed response. Agreement with the first does not automatically require agreement with the second.
Position A: Accept practical limits and argue that domestic needs should take priority.

Position B: Challenge the claimed impossibility by explaining how cooperation can extend assistance; also defend an international responsibility. Do not confuse helping many people with proving everyone can be reached.
Position C: Accept that universal help is difficult, but argue for domestic priorities alongside targeted international aid. Model M7 develops this position.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “People now change jobs more frequently, so governments should discourage this trend.” Position: “Job changes may reflect a healthy labour market, so discouraging them broadly is unjustified even if excessive turnover causes problems.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Separate the alleged FACT (frequent changes) from the proposed ACTION (discourage them). You may accept the first but reject the inference that the second is necessary. Address both claims explicitly to avoid an incomplete response.
Comparisons and absolute claims

For “A is more important than B”, compare their importance directly. You may prioritise one, consider them equally important, or explain when each matters. For “the best” or “the only” solution, test the strength of that claim. You are free to agree if you can support it; automatic disagreement is not a rule.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “The best way to reduce road accidents is to increase fines.” Thesis: “Higher fines can discourage dangerous driving, but enforcement and road design may be equally important.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Best” is a ranking claim; you must weigh this measure against credible alternatives rather than merely say fines help. The phrase “only way” would be even stronger and need broader support. Avoid an automatic yes/no without comparing mechanisms.
Make a judgement in an outweigh essay

Counting benefits and drawbacks is not enough. Compare their seriousness, scale, duration or reversibility. Two minor benefits may matter less than one serious drawback. Make the comparison explicit in a body paragraph and the conclusion.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “Do the benefits of online banking outweigh the drawbacks?” Benefit: convenience for many everyday transactions. Drawback: exclusion of people without digital access. Judgement: benefits may outweigh costs IF accessible alternatives are retained.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The assessment is not a headcount of positive and negative points. Compare who is affected, how serious the harm is and whether it is reversible. A well-argued judgement can be conditional and still answer “outweigh”.
Write introductions and conclusions simply
Opinion introduction: “Some people believe that [accurate paraphrase]. I largely agree because [main reasons].” Adapt the wording; do not force a memorised sentence onto an unsuitable task.
Two part introduction: “This trend is mainly driven by [reason]. I consider it largely [positive or negative] because [judgement].” The body must then answer both questions.

Conclusion: Restate the answer and the main reasoning briefly. A recommendation is optional and should follow from the discussion. Avoid “This essay will shed light on…” when you can state your answer directly.
Ready for practice: You can identify the task, choose a position and explain the job of each paragraph. Next, complete Exercises E1–E8 before checking the answer key.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Prompt: “Some believe school uniforms should be mandatory. To what extent do you agree?” Introduction: “School uniforms are often seen as a way to promote equality. I partly agree with compulsory uniforms because they can reduce visible differences, but strict rules can be costly.” Conclusion: “Overall, uniforms can be helpful, although schools should keep requirements affordable and flexible.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The introduction identifies the real issue and states a qualified stance. The conclusion returns to the SAME judgement without adding a new argument. You do not need a grand opening about “society nowadays” or a memorised “This essay will discuss…” formula.

guide.text: Part 3 Idea planning
Plan before you write
Practise a 5–8 minute plan before each essay. For early sessions, take longer if needed. Use keywords for planning, but complete sentences for the final essay.
A reusable planning worksheet
1. Question and scope What exactly is the topic? Which people, place or trend does it concern?
2. Instructions List every question you must answer. Circle words such as only, all and best.
3. Position Write one sentence giving your answer. For a two part task, answer both parts.
4. Body paragraph 1 Main point → why or how → example → result or link to the task.
5. Body paragraph 2 Main point → why or how → example → result or link to the task.
6. Final check Do the ideas differ? Does the plan cover the whole task and support your position?
Worked miniature plan on food waste
Task: Explain causes and solutions. Main answer: Poor purchasing plans and oversized portions create avoidable waste; better planning and flexible portions can reduce it.
Body 1: Unplanned purchases → too much perishable food; large portions → leftovers are discarded. Example: buying a discounted multipack that cannot be used before it spoils.
Body 2: Households check supplies and write shopping lists; restaurants offer smaller portions. Explain how each action reduces the matching source of waste. See Model M3.
How to use the topic bank

Prompts P1–P25 retain the practice topics from the guide, with consistent numbering. Cover the suggested plan first. Make your own plan, compare it with the suggestions, then add one example. Any defensible position is possible. Complete sample answers are at the end in the P1–P25 sample essays section.
Topic plans 1 to 3
P1 Shopping malls
Nowadays young people like spending much of their free time in shopping malls. Do the advantages of this development outweigh its disadvantages?
Outweigh essay. Possible view: The disadvantages are greater when shopping takes up too much leisure time.
Benefits: Malls provide meeting places and entertainment. Comparing prices can develop budgeting skills if young people follow a spending limit.
Drawbacks: Advertising may encourage overspending, while frequent shopping can replace exercise or low cost hobbies. Compare repeated financial and time costs with occasional enjoyment.
Limit: Do not assume every mall visit involves buying goods. Vocabulary: impulse purchases; consumer spending; leisure activities. Complete answer in the P1 Shopping malls section.
P2 Threats to animal species
Animal species are becoming extinct due to human activities on land and in the sea. What are the reasons and solutions?
Causes and solutions. Match each response to a source of harm.
Causes: Forest clearance removes habitats; overfishing reduces marine populations. Choose specific examples and explain the effect on survival or reproduction.
Solutions: Protect and restore habitats; enforce fishing limits and monitor catches. Name the responsible authorities and explain how enforcement changes behaviour.
Limit: A protected area needs management, not just a name. Vocabulary: habitat loss; overexploitation; conservation (bảo tồn). Complete answer in the P2 Threats to animal species section.
P3 Antisocial behaviour
These days, there has been an increase in antisocial behaviour and a lack of respect for people. What are the causes and what solutions can be taken?
Causes and solutions. Focus on behaviour such as harassment, aggression or public disorder.
Causes: Some children receive inconsistent guidance about respectful behaviour. Harmful conduct may also continue where rules are poorly enforced.
Solutions: Parents and schools can teach conflict resolution and model respect. Authorities can enforce proportionate penalties and provide clear reporting routes.

Limit: Avoid blaming an entire generation or treating quietness as antisocial behaviour. Vocabulary: social norms; parental guidance; law enforcement. Complete answer in the P3 Antisocial behaviour section.
Topic plans 4 to 6
P4 Work life balance
Not many people are able to achieve a balance between work and other aspects of life. What are the problems? What solutions can be suggested?
Problems and solutions. Discuss consequences, rather than using the whole first paragraph for causes.
Problems: Long hours reduce family time and opportunities to rest. Unequal domestic responsibilities can also restrict a partner’s career development.
Solutions: Employers can set reasonable workloads and clear contact hours. Household members can share domestic tasks more fairly to protect time for work and rest.
Limit: A pay rise alone may not reduce excessive hours. Vocabulary: support network; household responsibilities; career development. Complete answer in the P4 Work life balance section.
P5 Less family time
People are spending less time with their family members. What are the reasons for this phenomenon? What effects does it have?
Reasons and effects. Keep the causal chain visible.
Reasons: Conflicting work and study schedules reduce shared time. Individual screen use can displace conversation even when relatives are at home together.
Effects: Family members may have fewer opportunities to offer emotional support. Children may also receive less everyday guidance. Explain these as possibilities, not inevitable outcomes.

Limit: Online communication can also help relatives who live apart. Vocabulary: family bonding (gắn kết gia đình); competing priorities; emotional support. Complete answer in the P5 Less family time section.
P6 Fair university access

Some people think everyone has the right to access university education and governments should provide places for all students, no matter their financial background. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Opinion. Possible view: Support access based on ability and interest, without financial exclusion.
Body 1: Qualified students from low income households should not lose opportunities because of cost. Targeted grants can help them enrol and complete their studies.
Body 2: Capacity and academic requirements still matter. Governments can expand suitable places while also supporting vocational routes for students with other goals.

Limit: Financially fair access is not automatically universal free tuition or admission without prerequisites. Vocabulary: financial background; eligibility; targeted support. Complete answer in the P6 Fair university access section.
Topic plans 7 to 9
P7 Internet access and achievement
Internet access helps young people and workers achieve their education and work goals more easily than before. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Opinion. Possible view: Largely agree, while recognising unequal access and distractions.
Body 1: Search tools and online courses broaden access to learning. A student can revisit explanations and study topics unavailable locally.
Body 2: Video meetings and shared files make remote collaboration easier. Acknowledge that benefits depend on digital skills, reliable access and managing distractions.

Limit: Access creates opportunities; it does not guarantee success or equal outcomes. Vocabulary: remote collaboration; digital skills; flexible learning. Complete answer in the P7 Internet access and achievement section.
P8 Violence on screens
Violence on TV and in films is harmful, so governments should ban it. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Two linked claims. Possible view: Accept possible harm, but reject a blanket ban.
Body 1: Disturbing scenes may upset younger viewers or normalise aggression for some audiences. Explain the concern cautiously without claiming that all viewers become violent.
Body 2: Age ratings, parental controls and limits on graphic content can protect children while preserving choices for adults. Explain why targeted measures are preferable.

Limit: Recognising harm does not prove that complete prohibition is necessary. Vocabulary: graphic violence; impressionable (dễ bị ảnh hưởng); parental supervision. Complete answer in the P8 Violence on screens section.
P9 Technology and all societies
Modern technology is transforming how we work and is of benefit to all societies. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Two claims. Possible view: Agree that work is changing, but qualify the claim of universal benefit.
Body 1: Telecommunications enable remote work; automation reduces repetitive tasks. Explain one example in detail rather than listing devices.
Body 2: Benefits depend on infrastructure and training. Workers whose tasks are automated may need support, and communities without reliable connectivity may gain less.

Limit: Address “all societies” explicitly. Avoid claiming that a single tool solves every professional problem. Vocabulary: automation; retraining; unequal access. Complete answer in the P9 Technology and all societies section.
Topic plans 10 to 12
P10 Roads and public transport
Some people think it is more important to spend money on roads and motorways than on public transport systems. To what extent do you agree?
Comparison. Possible view: Maintain safe roads, but prioritise public transport in congested cities.
Body 1: Road repairs improve safety and support essential freight and bus services. Explain why maintenance remains necessary.
Body 2: Frequent, affordable buses or trains offer alternatives to private cars and help people who do not drive. Compare their value for moving large numbers of urban travellers.

Limit: Wider roads may attract additional traffic; neither type of investment fits every location. Vocabulary: congestion (ùn tắc); road maintenance; transit networks. Complete answer in the P10 Roads and public transport section.
P11 Old buildings
Many people think old buildings should be knocked down to give way to new buildings. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Opinion. Possible view: Assess buildings individually rather than demolishing them solely because of age.
Body 1: Historic structures can preserve distinctive architecture and support tourism. Restoration or reuse may protect their value while meeting current needs.
Body 2: Unsafe buildings with little heritage value may justify replacement if repair is impractical. Compare safety, cost and public benefit.

Limit: Old does not always mean unsafe, and new does not always mean better. Vocabulary: cultural heritage; restoration; craftsmanship (tay nghề thủ công). Complete answer in the P11 Old buildings section.
P12 Moving companies to the countryside
Traffic and housing problems could only be solved by moving large companies, factories and their employees to the countryside. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
An “only” claim. Possible view: Relocation may help, but it is not the sole solution.
Body 1: Moving some jobs can reduce pressure on city housing and commuter routes. However, it may create new travel needs and housing pressure in receiving areas.
Body 2: Better public transport, affordable housing near jobs and staggered working hours address problems without requiring all firms to move.

Limit: Explain how alternatives work, not simply that they exist. Vocabulary: relocation; urban planning (quy hoạch đô thị); housing supply. Complete answer in the P12 Moving companies to the countryside section.
Topic plans 13 to 15
P13 The purpose of sport
Many people believe that sports are only a form of recreation. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
An “only” claim. Possible view: Disagree because sport has purposes beyond entertainment.
Body 1: Regular participation can develop physical skills and provide a structured way to stay active. Training also requires persistence.
Body 2: Team activities can teach cooperation and bring communities together. Explain how shared practice and rules support these outcomes.
Limit: Acknowledge enjoyment; the disagreement concerns the word “only”. Vocabulary: recreation; discipline; community participation. Complete answer in the P13 The purpose of sport section.
P14 Financial aid and practical assistance

Some people think developing countries need financial help from international governments and organisations. Others think practical aid and advice are needed. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discussion. Possible view: Combine funding with locally appropriate expertise.
View 1: Money lets recipients pay for infrastructure, equipment and local priorities. Weak oversight can reduce its effectiveness; not all aid is a loan.
View 2: Training and technical advice build skills, but recommendations may fail without equipment or funding. Explain why combining resources and local knowledge is useful.

Limit: The best mix depends on the problem and local capacity. Vocabulary: financial assistance; technical expertise; recipient country. Complete answer in the P14 Financial aid and practical assistance section.
P15 Team and individual sports
Some people think team sports, like football, are more beneficial for children. Others prefer individual sports, like tennis or swimming. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discussion. Possible view: Both are valuable; suitability depends on the child and the setting.
View 1: Team sports practise communication and cooperation. Players must coordinate their actions and respond to shared success or failure.
View 2: Individual sports can develop self discipline and responsibility for progress. Conclude that access to both gives children different learning experiences.

Limit: Do not assume individual sports involve no coaches, teammates or social contact. Vocabulary: teamwork; self discipline; personal progress. Complete answer in the P15 Team and individual sports section.
Topic plans 16 to 18
P16 Food travelling long distances
Today food travels thousands of miles before it reaches customers. Why is this? Is this a positive or negative trend?
Two part question. Possible view: Benefits are substantial, but impacts depend on production and transport.
Reasons: Consumers want foods unavailable locally or out of season. International supply chains make trade possible across regions.
Evaluation: Imports increase choice and can strengthen supply security, while transport and storage create costs and some local producers face stronger competition. State an overall judgement.

Limit: Distance alone does not determine a food’s total environmental impact. Vocabulary: food security; trade barriers; transportation; local producers. Complete answer in the P16 Food travelling long distances section.
P17 Traditional dress and the past
Traditional dress and costumes are considered effective ways of maintaining links with the past. How effective can they be? What other ways help citizens connect with a country’s past?
Two questions. Evaluate effectiveness, then explain other methods.

Body 1: Clothing used in festivals can make cultural traditions visible and memorable. For example, the áo dài can prompt discussion of Vietnamese design and identity. Clothing alone may give limited historical detail.
Body 2: Museum visits, oral histories and school lessons explain context. Connect objects and stories to the people and events behind them.

Limit: Avoid presenting one costume as representing every person in a country. Vocabulary: cultural identity; artefacts; historical understanding. Complete answer in the P17 Traditional dress and the past section.
P18 Natural extinction and conservation
It is a natural process for animal species to become extinct. There is no reason why people should try to prevent this. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Two linked claims. Possible view: Natural extinction occurs, but that does not remove reasons for conservation.
Body 1: Accept that species have disappeared through natural environmental change. Distinguish this from avoidable pressures such as habitat destruction and overexploitation.
Body 2: Conservation can protect ecological relationships and reduce human caused losses. Explain why preventing avoidable harm is a reason to act.

Limit: Do not assume every extinction strengthens an ecosystem. Vocabulary: extinction (tuyệt chủng); endangered species; ecological balance. Complete answer in the P18 Natural extinction and conservation section.
Topic plans 19 to 21
P19 Economic growth and a clean environment
Some people say a country can be both economically successful and have a clean environment. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discussion. Possible view: The goals can coexist, but require effective policy and investment.
View 1: Production, transport and construction can create pollution and resource pressure. Cleaner systems have initial costs that some businesses struggle to meet.
View 2: Energy efficiency, wastewater treatment and cleaner production can reduce damage while supporting economic activity. Explain the role of regulation and investment.

Limit: Economic growth does not automatically finance protection or eliminate pollution. Vocabulary: environmental sustainability; trade off; cleaner production. Complete answer in the P19 Economic growth and a clean environment section.
P20 Global warming and deforestation
Some people believe global warming is today’s most pressing environmental problem. Others consider deforestation to have the most devastating impact. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discussion and comparison. Possible view: Climate change has broader effects, while forest protection remains essential.
View 1: Forest loss threatens habitats and affects communities that depend on forests. Explain why these local and wider effects deserve urgent attention.
View 2: A changing climate affects many regions and systems. Compare scale and duration, then acknowledge that deforestation and climate change are connected.

Limit: Do not dismiss deforestation as minor or suggest a local law alone solves it. Vocabulary: forest clearance; habitat protection; climate impacts. Complete answer in the P20 Global warming and deforestation section.
P21 Who should solve environmental problems
Solving environmental problems should be the responsibility of an international organisation rather than each national government. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Comparison. Possible view: Responsibility should be shared.
Body 1: International cooperation helps with cross border problems, common targets and support for countries with fewer resources.
Body 2: National and local authorities implement rules, monitor compliance and adapt measures to local needs. Explain why coordination cannot replace implementation.

Limit: Avoid treating international bodies as a single authority able to enforce every local decision. Vocabulary: international cooperation; local implementation; monitoring. Complete answer in the P21 Who should solve environmental problems section.
Topic plans 22 to 24
P22 Children becoming overweight
In many countries, children are becoming overweight and unhealthy. Some people think the government should have responsibility for solving this problem. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Opinion about responsibility. Possible view: Government has an important role, alongside families and schools.
Body 1: Public policy can improve access to safe activity spaces and support clear food information. Explain why individual households cannot supply these systems alone.
Body 2: Schools shape daily routines and parents influence meals and activities. Explain how their frequent contact can support public measures.

Limit: Do not spend a whole paragraph proving that children are overweight; answer who should act. Vocabulary: healthy habits; public facilities; shared responsibility. Complete answer in the P22 Children becoming overweight section.
P23 Exercise in cities
It is difficult for people in cities to get enough physical exercise. What are the causes and solutions?
Causes and solutions. Pair time barriers with practical changes.
Causes: Long commutes and work schedules leave limited time. Some neighbourhoods lack convenient, safe places for activity.
Solutions: Employers can support reasonable schedules and active breaks. Cities can improve walking routes, cycling connections and accessible parks so activity fits daily travel.

Limit: Avoid assuming that indoor exercise is inherently unsafe or that everyone can afford a gym. Vocabulary: city dwellers; accessible facilities; active travel. Complete answer in the P23 Exercise in cities section.
P24 Good news and bad news
The media should include more stories reporting good news rather than bad news. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Opinion. Possible view: Support more constructive reporting while keeping coverage of serious problems.
Body 1: Stories about community projects and useful discoveries can inform and encourage readers. Explain why reporting solutions can have public value.
Body 2: Reporting disasters, abuse or corruption helps people respond and hold institutions accountable. News selection should reflect public importance, not positivity alone.

Limit: Distinguish necessary negative news from sensational treatment. Vocabulary: balanced coverage; public interest; sensational headlines. Complete answer in the P24 Good news and bad news section.
Final topic and independent planning
P25 Newspapers and other media
Some people think newspapers are the best way to get news. Others believe other media platforms are better. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Discussion. Possible view: Evaluate reliability and purpose, rather than assuming one format is always best.
View 1: Newspapers can provide edited, detailed coverage and a focused reading experience. Explain the value of context and editorial checks.
View 2: Digital platforms can offer fast updates, video and broad access. However, readers need to verify sources. Conclude that credible reporting matters across formats.

Limit: Newspapers may publish online, so distinguish format from the organisation producing the news. Vocabulary: editorial standards; credibility; verification. Complete answer in the P25 Newspapers and other media section.
